IPT.evidence_source: [016_results] Participants in the CBT group showed significantly greater reductions in CDI scores from baseline to post-treatment compared to the control group (F(1, 80) = 12.5, p < .001, ηp2 = .13).

male_pct.evidence_source: [016_results] The mean age of the sample was 14.2 years (SD = 1.6), and 62% were female.

dxgive.evidence_source: [016_results] At baseline, the mean Children’s Depression Inventory (CDI) score was 25.3 (SD = 6.1), indicating moderate depression severity.

Source.evidence_source: [016_results] At baseline, the mean Children’s Depression Inventory (CDI) score was 25.3 (SD = 6.1), indicating moderate depression severity. [016_results] The mean Revised Children’s Manifest Anxiety Scale (RCMAS) score was 18.7 (SD = 5.2), and the mean Social Skills Rating System (SSRS) score was 98.1 (SD = 15.3). [016_results] No significant differences were found between the CBT and control groups on measures of family functioning (Family Assessment Device – General Functioning, FAD-GF) or self-esteem (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, RSES). [016_results] Mediation analyses revealed that changes in negative automatic thoughts, as measured by the Automatic Thoughts Questionnaire – Revised (ATQ-R), significantly mediated the relationship between CBT treatment and reductions in CDI scores (β = .35, p < .01).
